sections.markdown:
## C — Sharing the road part two: bicycles at signals that fail to detect them, mopeds, motorcycles and lane splitting or filtering, vulnerable road users and NEVs, passing, following and turning near commercial vehicles, railroad crossings, highway work zones and the zipper merge
Knowledge domain: how to share Minnesota roads with bicycles, mopeds, motorcycles, other vulnerable road users, neighborhood electric vehicles and commercial vehicles, how to cross railroad tracks safely, and how to drive through work zones and lane closures.

FACT_ID: sec08-F01 | anchor: A01
A bicyclist whose presence a traffic light fails to detect may go through after a reasonable wait, once fully stopped, if the red lasts unreasonably long or the signal seems broken, and no one is approaching close enough to be a hazard. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec08-F02 | anchor: A01
That undetected-bicycle defense covers only a charge of entering or crossing against a red light, not any other civil or criminal action. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec08-F03 | anchor: A01
Look for bicyclists in intersections, on sidewalks and at alleys and driveways, and take extra care around bicycle traffic at night. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec08-F04 | anchor: A01
A motorized bicycle, or moped, is defined by a top speed capability of 30 mph or less, and bicycle riding rules generally apply to it. [A01]
Why it matters: the moped speed cap is a likely numeric item.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec08-F05 | anchor: A01
Mopeds may not be ridden on sidewalks, on freeways, or in lanes and trails set aside for pedestrians and bicycles. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec08-F06 | anchor: A01
Because motorcycles are small, their speed and distance are hard to judge as they approach. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec08-F07 | anchor: A01
Leave at least as much following distance behind a motorcycle as behind any other vehicle, since a rider may have trouble controlling it and weave. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec08-F08 | anchor: A01
When moving into a lane ahead of a motorcycle, leave as much room behind your vehicle as you would for a car. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec08-F09 | anchor: A01
If a motorcyclist passes you, keep your lane position and speed and let the rider finish the pass. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec08-F10 | anchor: A01
Crowding a motorcyclist is illegal, and you must never drive beside a motorcycle in the same lane. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec08-F11 | anchor: A01
A motorcyclist may legally share your lane to pass you in slow or stopped traffic, and you must not block or try to stop them. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec08-F12 | anchor: A02
Lane splitting is legal only where two or more lanes run in the same direction with traffic moving, at no more than 25 mph and no more than 15 mph faster than the surrounding traffic. [A02]
Why it matters: splitting and filtering limits are easy to swap.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec08-F13 | anchor: A02
Lane filtering lets a motorcycle move between stopped vehicles, such as at a light or in a jam, where two or more lanes run the same way, at no more than 15 mph above the traffic speed. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec08-F14 | anchor: A02
The most common motorcycle-car crashes happen at urban intersections, many when a driver fails to yield and turns left across an oncoming motorcycle's path. [A02]
Why it matters: the left-turn crash pattern is a likely test item.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec08-F15 | anchor: A02
Right-of-way laws protect motorcyclists like everyone else, and motorcyclists may use high-occupancy vehicle lanes. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec08-F16 | anchor: A03
Vulnerable road users have less protection than people in cars and include riders of two- or three-wheeled vehicles, users of electric mobility devices, horseback riders, walkers and motorized scooter riders. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec08-F17 | anchor: A03
A neighborhood electric vehicle is a three- or four-wheeled electric vehicle with a top speed between 20 and 25 mph, and it must be titled and registered with Driver and Vehicle Services. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec08-F18 | anchor: A03
Any Class D license holder may drive a neighborhood electric vehicle, but only on streets with speed limits of 35 mph or less, and one may not be used for a road test. [A03]
Why it matters: the NEV street limit is a likely numeric item.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec08-F19 | anchor: A03
A commercial vehicle is a motor vehicle or combination weighing over 26,000 pounds that carries passengers or property, and every bus of any size, school buses included, counts too, as do smaller vehicles displaying hazardous materials placards. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec08-F20 | anchor: A03
Passing a commercial vehicle on a level highway takes three to five seconds longer than passing a car, and you still must be back in your lane before coming within 100 feet of oncoming traffic. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec08-F21 | anchor: A03
If you will exit or turn off soon, stay behind the commercial vehicle instead of passing it. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec08-F22 | anchor: A03
Commercial vehicles slow down going uphill, making them easier to pass, but speed up going downhill, so allow more distance for a downhill pass. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec08-F23 | anchor: A03
Finish a pass of a commercial vehicle quickly, return to your lane only once its front shows in your rearview mirror, and keep your speed afterward. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec08-F24 | anchor: A03
While a truck or bus is passing you, move to the far side of your lane, ease off slightly, and never speed up. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec08-F25 | anchor: A03
When meeting a commercial vehicle head-on, keep as far right as you can; the wind turbulence pushes the two vehicles apart, not together. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec08-F26 | anchor: A03
Large commercial vehicles often seem slower than they really are, and many car-truck crashes at intersections come from misjudging their speed and distance. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec08-F27 | anchor: A04
Cutting in close ahead of a bus or truck is especially dangerous, because you are likely in its blind spot and it cannot slow quickly enough to avoid you. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec08-F28 | anchor: A04
At 55 mph an average car can stop within 130 to 140 feet, while a fully loaded tractor-trailer may need more than 400 feet. [A04]
Why it matters: the stopping distance gap explains why you never cut in front of a truck.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec08-F29 | anchor: A04
Following a truck too closely blocks your view of the road ahead, so stay far enough back that the driver can see you in the side mirrors. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec08-F30 | anchor: A04
Always dim your headlights when following a commercial vehicle at night, because its large side mirrors reflect light into the driver's eyes. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec08-F31 | anchor: A04
When a commercial vehicle is merging it needs more time than a car to reach normal speed, so be ready to slow down or change lanes. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec08-F32 | anchor: A04
Stopped behind a commercial vehicle on an upgrade, leave room for it to roll back slightly as it starts, and sit on the left side of your lane where the driver can see you. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec08-F33 | anchor: A04
Many commercial vehicles swing wide for right turns, so never pass one on the right when it might be turning right. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec08-F34 | anchor: A04
A truck's no zones are blind spots where the driver may not see up to 20 feet ahead of the cab, along either side of the trailer, or up to 200 feet behind. [A04]
Why it matters: the no-zone distances are likely numeric items.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec08-F35 | anchor: A05
Because of a train's size and weight, most collisions between vehicles and trains kill the driver. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec08-F36 | anchor: A05
When crossing lights flash, bells ring or gates are down, do not cross, and stop at least 10 feet from the nearest rail or gate. [A05]
Why it matters: the rail stopping distance is a classic numeric item.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec08-F37 | anchor: A05
Cross the tracks only when traffic ahead has moved and you can clear them without having to stop within 10 feet beyond the rails. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec08-F38 | anchor: A05
Passenger vans, buses and larger trucks must stop at every railroad track even with no train present, and passing any vehicle within 100 feet of a railroad crossing is illegal. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec08-F39 | anchor: A05
After the last car of a train passes, wait until you are sure no second train is coming on another track, and look both ways at every crossing. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec08-F40 | anchor: A05
Never shift gears while crossing the tracks; in a manual transmission vehicle, shift down before you enter the crossing. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec08-F41 | anchor: A06
Every highway-rail crossing has a blue Emergency Notification System sign on the crossing posts or control box with a round-the-clock number for reporting an obstruction or problem that requires stopping trains. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec08-F42 | anchor: A06
In a work zone, disobeying a flag person or the speed limit brings a violation and a financial penalty. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec08-F43 | anchor: A06
Speeding in a work zone adds a $300 fine on top of the regular speeding ticket. [A06]
Why it matters: the work zone fine is a likely numeric item.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec08-F44 | anchor: A06
Where a work zone has no reduced speed limit posted, the ordinary posted limit still applies. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec08-F45 | anchor: A06
In a zipper merge, once a lane closed ahead sign appears and traffic backs up, stay in your lane to the merge point and then take turns merging into the open lane. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0057]

Misconceptions: motorcycle lane splitting and filtering are legal in Minnesota within set limits, so blocking a rider is wrong; a truck that looks slow may be moving faster than it seems; merging early is not the preferred method when a lane closes in heavy traffic; a stopped train is not the only danger, because a second train may follow on another track.
Mnemonics: split at no more than twenty-five and never more than fifteen over the traffic; trucks cannot see twenty feet in front or two hundred behind; stop ten from the rail and clear ten beyond it; NEVs stay on thirty-five or slower streets.
Glossary: lane splitting means a motorcycle passing within a lane in moving traffic; lane filtering means a motorcycle moving between stopped vehicles; no zone means a blind spot around a commercial vehicle; neighborhood electric vehicle means a small electric vehicle limited to low-speed streets; zipper merge means using both lanes to the merge point and taking turns; Emergency Notification System means the blue sign at a rail crossing with a number for reporting problems.
Dynamic facts: the work zone speeding fine is an amount set by law that can change; recheck it against an official DPS source before each release.

corpus_stability.reason: The Minnesota Driver’s Manual prints a single edition line (June 2026) on its front cover and opens with a New laws and information chapter that collects recent changes in one place, with no sign of more than one rewrite per year in the selected pages.
